title: Rewrite a Vault Policy to Least Privilege
intro: The shop application's Vault policy was written in a hurry: it grants everything on every path, including sudo. With it, a bug in one app can read every team's secrets, rewrite policies, and disable audit logging. Replace it with what the app actually needs: read its own secrets, and get its database credentials.

steps.prompt:
Rewrite shop-app.hcl so it contains exactly three path blocks and no wildcard-everything rule:

(1) path "secret/data/shop/*"       capabilities = ["read"]
(2) path "secret/metadata/shop/*"   capabilities = ["list", "read"]
(3) path "database/creds/shop-readonly"   capabilities = ["read"]

The app must not be able to write, delete, or use sudo anywhere.
steps.explanation: The app can read its own secrets, list their names, and request read-only database credentials. Everything else is denied by default.
steps.why: Vault denies whatever no policy grants, so least privilege means listing only what's needed. The original gave 'sudo' on '*', which allows root-protected operations such as changing audit devices and policies: an attacker who took over the app could have covered their tracks. Three details matter. The 'data/' and 'metadata/' segments: policies are matched against the real API path, and leaving them out is the usual reason a correct-looking policy returns 'permission denied'. Reading database/creds/shop-readonly is a 'read' even though it creates a database user, because that's how the API models it. And the glob only matches at the end of a path: 'secret/data/shop/*' covers everything below shop/, and nothing in another team's subtree. Check a policy with 'vault token capabilities <path>' using a token that carries it, for both a path that should work and one that shouldn't.
